quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on the vocabulary of colour-and-weave effects: hairlines, hound's tooth, bird's eye, colour order and how the face shows colour.

questions.q: On the face of the cloth, where does the warp colour show?
options: Wherever the pick is on top
Wherever the end is lifted over the pick
questions.explain: A lifted end lies over the weft, so its colour is seen; where the end is down the pick is on top and the weft colour shows instead.

questions.q: What is a colour-and-weave effect?
options: A stripe made by changing the weave across the width
A pattern produced by combining a colour order of ends and picks with a simple weave, which neither the weave nor the colouring would show alone
A figure woven on a jacquard
questions.explain: Hairlines, hound's tooth and bird's eye come from the colour order laid over a plain weave or twill; the weave itself is unchanged.

questions.q: Which combination gives vertical hairlines in the lecture?
questions.explain: Plain weave coloured 1 dark 1 light in the warp, with the weft light-dark, gives dark lines warp-way. 2/2 twill with 4 and 4 is hound's tooth.

questions.q: The classic hound's tooth (dog-tooth) pattern is produced by:
options: 2/2 twill with 4 dark, 4 light in both warp and weft
questions.explain: Four dark, four light in both directions on a 2/2 twill is the lecture's hound's tooth. Plain 1 and 1 gives hairlines.

questions.q: The bird's eye or step effect in the lecture comes from:
questions.explain: Plain weave coloured 2 and 2 in both directions gives the small bird's eye / step. 2/2 twill with 1 and 1 gives the small step effect, a different drawing in the lecture.

questions.q: On plain weave with 1 and 1 colouring, shifting the weft colour order by one pick turns the vertical hairlines into horizontal ones.
questions.explain: The lecture's two hairline drawings use the same weave and warp order; only the weft order is moved one pick, and the dark lines swing from warp-way to weft-way.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill with 2 and 2 colouring in both directions gives:
questions.explain: The lecture's drawing of 2/2 twill with 2 and 2 shows hairlines running weft-way. Hound's tooth needs 4 and 4 on the same twill.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill with 1 and 1 colouring gives:
questions.explain: On the 2/2 twill the 1 and 1 order breaks the diagonal into a small step effect; vertical hairlines need plain weave.

questions.q: CAD systems treat a colour-and-weave effect by keeping the weave as a plain 2/2 twill and storing the colour order separately.
questions.explain: The lecture notes that the companion gives the colour order separately and leaves the weave as an ordinary 2/2 twill, which is how CAD systems handle these effects.

questions.q: In the lecture's original hex encoding of hound's tooth, where was the colour order kept?
options: In the first row of the hex design
questions.explain: The original encoding put the colour order in the first row ($3C0 … −10 and $0F0 … −10); the companion separates it from the weave.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Repeat sizes, face proportions and what changes when the colour order or the weave is altered.

questions.q: How is the repeat of a colour-and-weave effect found?
options: It is the lowest common multiple of the weave repeat and the colour repeat
It is the weave repeat plus the colour repeat
questions.explain: The pattern only returns when both the weave and the colouring return together, so the repeat is the LCM: for 2/2 twill (4) with 4 and 4 (8) it is 8.

questions.q: The hound's tooth of 2/2 twill with 4 and 4 colouring repeats on:
questions.explain: The 4-end twill and the 8-end colour order both close on 8, which is why the lecture draws it on 8 × 8. 4 is only the weave repeat.

questions.q: Plain weave with 1 and 1 colouring has a true repeat of:
questions.explain: Both the plain weave and the 1 and 1 order repeat on 2, so the effect repeats on 2 × 2; the 8 × 8 drawing simply shows several repeats.

questions.q: In the plain-weave vertical hairline, why does a column of dark appear under a dark end?
options: Because the reed groups the dark ends
Because the weft is all dark
Because the dark end shows when it is up, and when it is down the pick on top is also dark
Because the dark end is lifted on every pick
questions.explain: The lecture's own note: warp dark-light, weft light-dark, so wherever the dark end is down the dark pick covers it. The column is dark on every pick.

questions.q: Keep the 2 and 2 colouring but change the weave from plain to 2/2 twill. The effect changes from:
options: Bird's eye / step to weft-way hairlines
questions.explain: The lecture shows plain 2 and 2 as bird's eye and 2/2 twill 2 and 2 as weft-way hairlines: same colour order, different weave, different pattern.

questions.q: Half the ends and half the picks are dark and the weave is a balanced 2/2 twill. What fraction of the face is dark?
questions.explain: Half the face is warp (half of it dark) and half is weft (half dark): 0.5 × 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.5 = 50 %. The colour order rearranges the dark, it does not change the amount.

questions.q: A 3/1 twill with an all-dark warp and all-light weft shows a face that is 75 % dark.
questions.explain: The 3/1 twill puts warp on 3 picks in 4 of the face, and all the warp is dark, so 75 % of the face is dark; this is a weave effect, not a colour-and-weave effect.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill is coloured 3 dark, 3 light in both directions. The repeat of the effect is:
questions.explain: LCM of the 4-end weave and the 6-end colour order is 12. Taking only the colour repeat (6) or adding 4 + 3 (7) are common slips.

questions.q: If every dark thread is swapped for light and every light for dark, in both warp and weft, the cloth shows:
options: The same pattern in negative (dark and light exchanged)
questions.explain: Every square that showed dark now shows light and vice versa, so the arrangement of the pattern is unchanged; only its colours are reversed.

questions.q: The weft colour appears on the face wherever:
options: The end is down, so the pick lies on top
questions.explain: A pick is seen only where it crosses over an end that is down. Where the end is up, the warp colour hides it.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Working out repeats, counting dark squares, face proportions with mixed colour orders and reading the lecture's hex codes.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill (4-end repeat) is coloured 4 dark, 4 light in warp and weft. On how many ends does the hound's tooth effect repeat?
questions.explain: The colour order repeats on 8 and the weave on 4, which divides 8, so the LCM is 8 ends (and 8 picks).

questions.q: A 2/2 twill is coloured 3 dark, 3 light. On how many ends does the effect repeat?
questions.explain: LCM of 4 (weave) and 6 (colour order) = 12 ends.

questions.q: Plain weave is coloured 3 dark, 3 light in both directions. On how many picks does the effect repeat?
questions.explain: LCM of 2 (plain weave) and 6 (colour order) = 6 picks.

questions.q: The hound's tooth is drawn on 8 ends × 8 picks with 4 dark ends, 4 light ends, 4 dark picks and 4 light picks on a 2/2 twill. How many of the 64 squares show dark?
questions.explain: Half the warp-faced squares are dark and half the weft-faced squares are dark, so 32 of 64 are dark whatever the arrangement.

questions.q: A 3/1 twill is woven with all-dark warp and all-light weft. What percentage of the face is dark?
questions.explain: Warp covers 3 ÷ 4 = 75 % of the face and all of it is dark.

questions.q: Plain weave is woven with an all-dark warp and a weft coloured 1 dark, 1 light. What percentage of the face is dark?
questions.explain: Plain weave shows 50 % warp (all dark) plus 50 % weft, of which half is dark: 50 + 25 = 75 %.

questions.q: The hex code $3C0 −10 is read as a 10-end row (bits 0011 1100 0000, padding on the right). How many ends in that row are marked?
questions.explain: The 1-bits fall on ends 3, 4, 5 and 6: four ends. The last two zero bits are the padding beyond end 10.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of the hex number $3C0?
The row $0F0 −10 (bits 0000 1111 0000, padded on the right) marks which ends?
questions.explain: The most significant bit is end 1, so 0000 covers ends 1 to 4 and 1111 covers ends 5 to 8. Reading from the right gives the wrong 'ends 7 to 10'.

questions.q: Plain weave, warp coloured dark-light from end 1, weft light-dark from pick 1; pick 1 lifts the odd ends. What colour shows at end 2 on pick 1?
questions.explain: End 2 is light and is down on pick 1, so the pick on top is seen; pick 1 is light. Either way the square is light, which is why the light columns stay light throughout.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Running colour-and-weave effects in the mill: which weave and colour order to set, what goes wrong and the cheapest way to get a pattern.

questions.q: A buyer orders hound's tooth. The loom is weaving plain weave with a 4 dark, 4 light warp. What must change?
options: Nothing; plain weave 4 and 4 is hound's tooth
The weave to 2/2 twill, with the weft also coloured 4 and 4
questions.explain: Hound's tooth is 2/2 twill with 4 and 4 in both directions. Plain weave with the same colouring gives a different, blockier effect.

questions.q: A sample meant to show vertical hairlines comes off the loom with horizontal ones. The most likely cause is:
options: The warp was drawn in the wrong healds
The weft colour order started on the wrong colour, shifting it by one pick
questions.explain: The lecture shows that the same weave and warp order with the weft order moved one pick gives horizontal lines. Check which colour the weft selector starts with.

questions.q: A designer wants a new pattern on a loom that is already set up for 2/2 twill, without touching the peg plan. The simplest route is:
options: Change the colour order of warp and weft, e.g. 4 and 4 for hound's tooth or 2 and 2 for weft-way hairlines
questions.explain: Colour-and-weave effects keep the weave fixed and vary only the colour order, so the pegging and draft are untouched.

questions.q: A customer wants fine hairlines running weft-way on a 2/2 twill cloth. Which colouring do you set?
questions.explain: The lecture's 2/2 twill with 2 and 2 gives weft-way hairlines; 1 and 1 on the twill gives a small step and 4 and 4 gives hound's tooth.

questions.q: How should hound's tooth be entered in a CAD system, following the lecture?
options: As a single 8 × 8 weave with the colours drawn into the lifts
As a hex list with the colours in the first row
As a 2/2 twill plus a warp order 4 dark 4 light and a weft order 4 dark 4 light held separately
questions.explain: The companion separates colour order from weave, which is how CAD systems work; the old hex with the colour order in the first row is the method it replaced.

questions.q: Colour-and-weave effects such as hound's tooth need a jacquard loom.
questions.explain: They are built on plain weave or 2/2 twill, which need only 2 or 4 healds; the pattern comes from the colour order, so a tappet or dobby loom is enough.

questions.q: During a 1 and 1 hairline run the weaver loads a cop of the wrong colour so the weft order is thrown out by one pick for a stretch. What appears in the cloth?
options: The cloth becomes plain in colour
A bar where the hairlines switch from vertical to horizontal
questions.explain: Shifting the weft order by one pick converts vertical hairlines into horizontal ones, so the mis-threaded stretch shows as a clear bar of the other effect.

questions.q: Which is the cheaper way to give a plain cloth a small all-over pattern: changing the colour order of the yarns, or changing to a figured weave needing extra healds?
options: The figured weave, because yarn colours cost extra
The colour order, because the weave, draft and pegging stay the same
questions.explain: A colour-and-weave effect only changes which cones go on the creel and the weft selection; a figured weave means more healds, a new draft and slower weaving.

questions.q: The warp is coloured 1 dark, 1 light but the weft is all light, in plain weave. What does the face show?
options: Broken (dotted) dark lines warp-way, because the dark end shows only where it is lifted
questions.explain: Under a dark end the square is dark only on the picks where that end is up; where it is down the light pick shows. The lecture's solid hairline needs the dark pick to cover the dark end when it is down.

questions.q: At which stage of production is the warp colour order fixed?
options: At warping, when the cones are placed on the creel in order
questions.explain: The order of ends is set when the warp is made; the weft order is set on the loom by the selector or cop sequence. Neither can be changed in finishing.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across the lecture: two-step face proportions, repeat logic, the old hex encoding and the slips students make most.

questions.q: Why can one weave give two completely different patterns with two colour orders?
options: Because the colour seen on each square depends on both the lift and the colour of the thread on top, so rearranging the colours rearranges the pattern
Because the weave changes with the colour
questions.explain: The weave fixes which thread is on top in each square; the colour order fixes what colour that thread is. Changing either changes the picture.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill is woven with the warp coloured 1 dark, 1 light and an all-light weft. What percentage of the face is dark?
questions.explain: The 2/2 twill shows 50 % warp, half of which is dark: 50 × 0.5 = 25 %. The light weft adds no dark.

questions.q: A student says hound's tooth repeats on 4 ends because the 2/2 twill repeats on 4. What is wrong?
options: The colour order 4 and 4 repeats on 8, so the effect repeats on the LCM, 8 ends
questions.explain: After 4 ends the twill has returned but the colours have not (the next 4 ends are the other colour). Both return together only at 8.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill is coloured 6 dark, 6 light in both directions. On how many ends does the effect repeat?
questions.explain: The colour order repeats on 12 and the weave on 4, which divides 12, so the LCM is 12.

questions.q: In the lecture's old hex encoding, $3C0 … −10 and $0F0 … −10 are the first rows of the designs, carrying the colour order rather than a pick of the weave.
questions.explain: The lecture says the hound's tooth was encoded with the colour order in the first row; the companion drops this and stores the colour order separately.

questions.q: Plain weave, warp dark-light from end 1, weft dark-light from pick 1 (pick 1 dark, lifting the odd ends). What effect results?
questions.explain: On pick 1 the lifted odd ends are dark and the down even ends show the dark pick: a dark row. On pick 2 everything shows light. Rows alternate dark and light: horizontal hairlines.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a colour-and-weave effect?
options: Hound's tooth from 2/2 twill with 4 and 4
A stripe made by weaving 4/1 satin beside 1/4 sateen in one-colour yarn
Hairlines from plain weave with 1 and 1 colouring
Bird's eye from plain weave with 2 and 2
questions.explain: The satin/sateen stripe is a weave effect: the pattern comes from changing the weave, not the colour order. The other three keep one weave and vary the colours.

questions.q: A 3/1 twill is woven with the warp coloured 1 dark, 1 light and an all-light weft. What percentage of the face is dark? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: The 3/1 twill shows 75 % warp on the face; half of that warp is dark: 75 × 0.5 = 37.5 %.

questions.q: Why do hairlines on plain weave with 1 and 1 colouring run either warp-way or weft-way, never diagonally?
options: Because the yarns are too fine
Because plain weave has no diagonal; the direction is set only by whether the weft order is in phase or shifted by one pick
questions.explain: The lecture's two drawings differ only in the weft phase: in one the dark columns are continuous, in the other the dark rows. A diagonal would need a twill to carry it.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill is woven with an all-dark warp and an all-light weft. What does the face show?
options: The ordinary 2/2 twill diagonal in two colours, with no new colour-and-weave pattern
questions.explain: With one colour per thread system the face simply shows the weave itself in two colours. A colour-and-weave effect needs a colour order within the warp and weft.
